findings.claim: The peripheral route uses cues like credibility, emotion, and association
findings.failure_mode: cue misplaced: the source lists credibility as a Yale source feature; its peripheral-route cues are positive emotions and celebrity endorsement
findings.evidence: Deep 287: 'peripheral route uses cues like celebrity endorsement and emotional association'. Source 23448-23451 (peripheral) and 23388-23392 (credibility under Yale source features).
findings.fix: correct: The peripheral route uses cues like celebrity endorsement and positive emotional association

findings.claim: partly because compliance becomes consistent with the actor's self-perception (Freedman and Fraser)
findings.failure_mode: mechanism reworded into self-perception terms; the source gives the consistency principle (past behaviour and commitment), citing Cialdini
findings.evidence: Deep 287: 'exploits consistency'. Source 23480-23482: 'Research on this technique also illustrates the principle of consistency (Cialdini, 2001): Our past behavior often directs our future behavior, and we have a desire to maintain consistency once we have committed to a behavior.'
findings.fix: correct: partly because people want to stay consistent with a behaviour they have committed to (Freedman and Fraser; the consistency principle, Cialdini)

findings.claim: The converse — door-in-the-face — works through reciprocal concession. (Source: Ch 12.3)
findings.failure_mode: technique imported from outside the source and cited to Ch 12.3; 'door-in-the-face' does not occur in the source or the deep ref
findings.evidence: grep -i 'door-in-the-face' and 'door in the face' in sources/converted/openstax-psychology-2e.md: 0 hits. Deep 287 carries foot-in-the-door only.
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: Fairness of the processes determining outcomes predicts retaliation, aggression, and commitment. ... Process matters as much as outcome for sustaining stakeholder relationships.
findings.failure_mode: outcome list extended ('commitment') and a process-versus-outcome weighting added that the source does not make
findings.evidence: Deep 357: 'Procedural justice ... predicts retaliation and aggression; Greenberg's experiments showed that adequate explanations of pay decisions reduced theft'. Source 26930-26940 (workplace-violence triggers; Greenberg 1993).
findings.fix: correct: Fairness of the processes determining outcomes predicts retaliation and aggression. Adequate explanations of decisions reduced theft compared to curt explanations in Greenberg's experiments. For stakeholder relationships, the process deserves design attention alongside the outcome.

findings.claim: What structures will counter implicit bias (structured criteria, blind evaluation, counter-stereotypic exposure)?
findings.failure_mode: applied guidance resting on a premise absent from the source: counter-stereotypic exposure as an implicit-bias remedy does not appear in the source text
findings.evidence: Source mentions 'counterstereotypical' only in a reference-list title (41696). Deep 299, 351: superordinate goals; contact under equal status, common goals, cooperation, institutional support.
findings.fix: correct: What structures will counter implicit bias (structured criteria, blind evaluation, intergroup contact under the four conditions)?

findings.claim: Curt explanations corrode commitment.
findings.failure_mode: outcome misdescribed: in the source's Greenberg study curt explanations increased theft; commitment is not measured
findings.fix: correct: Curt explanations invite retaliation (in Greenberg's study, more theft).

findings.claim: intermittent acknowledgement sustains better than constant praise that can become invisible
findings.failure_mode: the 'constant praise can become invisible' premise is not in the source; the source says continuous reinforcement is the quickest way to teach a new behaviour and intermittent (variable-ratio) schedules resist extinction
findings.evidence: Deep 122-124 (variable ratio most extinction-resistant). Source 11372-11374: continuous reinforcement 'is the quickest way to teach someone a behavior, and it is especially effective in training a new behavior'.
findings.fix: correct: continuous acknowledgement helps a new behaviour take hold; intermittent acknowledgement then sustains it better

findings.claim: Relationships sustain through proximity, similarity, and reciprocity.
findings.failure_mode: formation and maintenance factors merged: the source names proximity and similarity as formation factors and reciprocity and self-disclosure as maintenance factors
findings.evidence: Deep 309: 'Proximity is the single most influential factor in relationship formation, with similarity another important factor ... Reciprocity and self-disclosure maintain relationships'.
findings.fix: correct: Relationships form through proximity and similarity and are maintained through reciprocity and self-disclosure.

findings.section: What to Look For (Persuasion runs through pure rationality)
findings.claim: peripheral cues (credibility, emotion, identity) ... attend to ... the audience factors (motivation, attention) of the Yale framework
findings.failure_mode: framework contents misstated: motivation is not a Yale audience factor (the source lists attention, intelligence, self-esteem, age; motivation belongs to ELM's central route), and 'identity' and 'credibility' are not the source's peripheral cues
findings.evidence: Deep 287. Source 23407-23408: 'Features of the audience that affect persuasion are attention ..., intelligence, self-esteem ..., and age'. Source 23448-23451 (peripheral cues).
findings.fix: correct: peripheral cues (celebrity, positive emotion) are operating where central-route assumptions are being made. Follow-up: attend to the Yale source factors (credibility, attractiveness) and audience factors (attention, intelligence, self-esteem, age), and to whether the audience is motivated and analytical enough for the central route (ELM).

findings.section: What to Look For (Engagement decisions pattern with group membership)
findings.claim: Follow-up: structured criteria; counter-stereotypic exemplar exposure; deliberate inclusion of low-similarity voices.
findings.failure_mode: same unsupported premise as D005
findings.evidence: As D005.
findings.fix: correct: Follow-up: structured criteria; intergroup contact under the four conditions; deliberate inclusion of low-similarity voices.

findings.section: What to Look For (Fair process skipped)

findings.failure_mode: outcome list extended ('erosion of commitment') and a claim of outcome-independence the source does not make
findings.evidence: Deep 357 (retaliation and aggression; theft).
findings.fix: correct: the cost is retaliation and aggression (in Greenberg's study, theft)

findings.claim: central-route persuasion and the Elaboration Likelihood Model (Ch 12.4), contact theory's four conditions (Ch 12.5)

findings.evidence: Deep 287 (ELM, Ch 12.3); deep 351 (Pettigrew and Tropp four conditions, Ch 13.3); source 26813-26823 (Ch 13.3). Distillation lines 22 and 36 cite Ch 12.3 and Ch 13.3.
findings.fix: correct: central-route persuasion and the Elaboration Likelihood Model (Ch 12.3), contact theory's four conditions (Ch 13.3)

findings.claim: The fundamental attribution error (Ch 12.1), central-route persuasion and the ELM, contact theory's four conditions, procedural justice (Ch 13.3), and Bandura's four elements of behaviour change (Ch 6.4) are all [AP]-marked passages in the deep ref.
findings.failure_mode: marker account wrong for most items: only the ELM passage is [AP]; the four contact conditions and procedural justice are [BT]; the FAE definition is [V] (as the distillation itself says at line 198); Bandura's four processes sit in an unmarked sentence and are processes of observational learning, not of behaviour change generally
findings.evidence: Deep 287 ELM [AP]; 351 contact [BT]; 357 procedural justice [BT]; 476 FAE [V]; 128 Bandura (four processes unmarked, Bobo doll [BT]).
findings.fix: correct: The ELM passage is [AP] in the deep ref; the contact conditions and Greenberg's procedural-justice study are [BT]; the fundamental attribution error definition is [V]; Bandura's four processes of observational learning (Ch 6.4) are paraphrase.

findings.claim: Implicit bias plus homophily plus the team halo effect produce decisions that pattern with demographics rather than merit.
findings.failure_mode: the team halo effect concerns team credit versus individual blame, not demographic patterning
findings.evidence: Source 26765-26767: 'Teams are given credit for their successes, but individuals within a team are blamed for team failures'. Deep 349.
findings.fix: correct: Implicit bias plus homophily produce decisions that pattern with demographics rather than merit; the team halo effect separately skews blame toward individuals.

findings.claim: Greenberg's work shows that perceived process fairness predicts retaliation and aggression independent of outcome quality.
findings.failure_mode: overgeneralised: the source's Greenberg study varied only the explanation of a pay rate and measured theft; it did not test independence from outcome quality
findings.fix: correct: Greenberg's work shows that curt rather than full explanations of a pay decision increased theft; procedural justice predicts retaliation and aggression (Ch 13.3).

findings.claim: Behaviour change requires Bandura's four elements (attention, retention, reproduction, motivation)
findings.failure_mode: scope widened: the four processes are what learning through modelling depends on, not requirements for behaviour change in general
findings.evidence: Deep 128: 'learning through modelling depends on attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation'.
findings.fix: correct: Learning through modelling depends on Bandura's four processes (attention, retention, reproduction, motivation) and on ongoing reinforcement, not just an effective one-time pitch.

findings.claim: Cialdini's six principles of influence | Reciprocity, commitment-and-consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity overlap with Psychology 2e's persuasion content
findings.failure_mode: enumerates a framework held neither as a corpus reference nor in the source; the source cites Cialdini only for foot-in-the-door and the consistency principle
findings.evidence: Source 23475, 23481 (Cialdini 2001: foot-in-the-door; consistency). Deep 463 lists Cialdini among Ch 12.3 persuasion anchors [BT]; no six-principles list.
findings.fix: correct: Cialdini (cited in Ch 12.3) | Psychology 2e cites Cialdini for foot-in-the-door and the consistency principle (Ch 12.3); his wider influence framework is not held in this corpus.

findings.claim: Many findings in social psychology (Milgram, Zimbardo, Asch) have faced replication challenges or ethical review since original publication; the source notes some of these caveats but not all.
findings.failure_mode: only the Zimbardo caveat is in the deep ref; 'but not all' imports outside knowledge; and for Milgram the source reports that partial replications matched the original, so grouping it under replication challenges misleads
findings.evidence: Deep 281 (Zimbardo: not fully replicated). Source 23644-23649 (Asch: conformity may have declined; replications show it varies with age, gender, socio-cultural background); 23716-23719 (Burger 2009 and Dolinski et al. 2017: 'results that were consistent with Milgram's original work'); 1726-1734 (Milgram's deception catalysed ethics guidelines).
findings.fix: correct: The source notes that Zimbardo's findings have not been fully replicated, that Asch-style conformity varies with age, gender and socio-cultural background and may have declined, that partial replications of Milgram matched the original, and that Milgram's deception helped prompt modern research-ethics rules. | cycle-to-deep: source 23644-23649, 23716-23719, 1726-1734

notes: No [V] quotations or blockquotes appear in this distillation (it says so); the protocol asks open-nc distillations for 2-5 verbatim blockquotes, so the verbatim register is missing rather than wrong. Integration checks: OB row matches OB deep 358-464 (French and Raven power bases, Salancik-Pfeffer resource dependence, Thomas conflict modes, BATNA); Tajfel and Turner (source 24248, Ch 12.5) and Bandura rows match. The 'Tyler' and 'Kelley's covariation model' pointers in rows 170 and 172 are pointers to outside literature, not claims about the source, and were graded FAITHFUL. Deep-ref note (not graded here): deep 351 says contact 'reduces prejudice when contact occurs under conditions of equal status...', while the source (26813-26823) reports a moderate effect that was 'enhanced' under those conditions; Key Concept 11 inherits that tightening. Most serious: D027 (licence stated as CC BY 4.0), D003 (door-in-the-face imported), and the cluster of chapter mis-cites in the borrowed-through list (D019-D024).
